name: Jamal Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing politics and economics at Redfield, about forty minutes on the train from home. Monday to Thursday it's lectures and seminars, and Friday I'm in the library. Weekends I stack shelves at Millbrook Foods, eight hours on Saturday and six on Sunday. I'm tired by Wednesday, but I like the seminars, where people actually argue.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got a scholarship for the top results, but it only covers part of the fees, so I have loans for the rest. I live at home with my mum, who drives a bus, and my sister Mika, who's fourteen. I give mum a bit from my wages every week and I have maybe three weeks of spending money saved. Nobody in my family has been to university, so I feel I have to make it count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hype that bosses use as an excuse to cut staff. At the shop they've put in self-checkouts and nobody got a pay rise. Friends use chatbots for essays and I tell them they're only teaching themselves to be lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even a quiet version makes me nervous. My money is thin: loans, a weekend wage and no family cushion. If the shop loses even one shift, I can't pay mum my share. Graduate jobs are already scarce around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both shifts, keep doing the reading and apply for a summer placement at the council. I'd also start going to the students' union advice night, because a few people there know about hardship funds. I wouldn't change how I study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired and a bit tense. I like my course, but I'm always counting hours and pounds. I'd call it steady pressure rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your shifts. What happens to the household if Millbrook Foods cuts weekend hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut the Sunday, I'd lose about ninety pounds a month. Mum would say keep the money for yourself, but she's already stretching. I'd pick up cleaning work from my aunt before I'd touch my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Is that a choice, or just how it's turned out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a choice. I don't trust something that writes things I can't check, and I'm slow with new software anyway. Nobody in my seminars would respect work they knew a machine wrote, and I want my marks to be mine.

say: I'd tell friends this is **hype** that bosses use to excuse cutting staff.
At the shop I'd point at self-checkouts: **no pay rise** came with them.
think: Even a quiet version worries me, because my **money is thin** and one lost shift hurts.
Graduate jobs are scarce here already, and I'd have **no cushion** if I missed one.
do: Keep both **weekend shifts** at Millbrook Foods and keep up the reading.
Apply for a **summer placement** at the council.
Go to the students' union **hardship fund** advice night.
feel: Tired and **tense**, always counting hours and pounds, but not panicking.
S0.quote: I like my course, but I'm always counting hours and pounds. I'd call it steady pressure rather than panic.
fieldNote: His worries are about **shifts and loans**, not AI, even in the calm scenario.
Avoids AI on principle and trusts unions and public help over firms.
Says he would lean on his aunt's cleaning work before borrowing more.

steps.text: Keep both weekend shifts at Millbrook Foods
Ask the students' union about the hardship fund
Apply for a summer placement at the council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and rules. If firms replace writers and checkers, they should pay a tax that funds retraining. People can't be told to just adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one scares me properly. Economics and law graduates do exactly the writing and checking the card talks about, so fewer entry jobs will exist when I finish in three years. I'd be competing with software for the same junior roles. I also can't afford to fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the students' union campaign on jobs and AI, and I'd stop assuming a business or politics degree leads to a desk. I'd look at public sector and policy work, where humans are still wanted. I'd keep my shifts, because that wage is what keeps me here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I can picture the rejection emails already. But I'm angry too, because the people who profit won't be the ones paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the thinking tasks on the card do you expect to hit your own degree first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reports, summaries, case checking. A first-year essay is exactly what these tools do, so I'd guess the graduate version of that job goes first. I haven't touched the tools, so I'd be starting behind my own classmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your university or the government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the university to teach us honestly what jobs exist at the end. And I'd want the government to guarantee retraining that pays a living wage, so I don't have to choose between rent and a course.

say: I'd say we need **unions and rules**, and firms replacing staff should fund retraining.
People can't just be told to **adapt**, so I'd push for public support.
think: Entry-level writing and checking is exactly what I'd apply for, so **fewer jobs** will be waiting in three years.
I'm **starting behind** classmates because I've never used the tools.
do: Join the students' union **campaign** on jobs and AI.
Look at **public sector** and policy work where people are still wanted.
Keep my **shifts**, since that wage keeps me at university.
feel: **Anxious**, picturing rejection emails, and angry that profits go to firms, not people like me.
S1.quote: I'd be competing with software for the same junior roles. I also can't afford to fail.
fieldNote: He is **angry** more than frightened, and blames firms rather than technology.
His reluctance with AI tools is a real disadvantage he admits.
Turns to collective routes first: union, university, state retraining.

steps.text: Join the students' union campaign on jobs and AI
Write to my MP about funded retraining
Research public sector and policy graduate schemes
Keep the Saturday and Sunday shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a crime. Nobody has voted for this and nobody is ready, not the government, not the unions, not my uni. I'd demand an emergency plan for income before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be in my second year when it lands, with a debt and a degree for jobs that software does. I'd feel I picked the wrong thing at the wrong time. My family can't catch me, so I'd have nothing to fall back on at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know what I'd do. I'd keep my shifts as long as they exist, and I'd ask the course office whether I can pause and not take more loan. I'd go to every union meeting going, because alone I'd be useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd probably not sleep much. Mostly I'd feel cheated, because I did everything right and worked hard for the grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what is the first thing you would do differently at university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating the degree as a plan. Probably switch to anything with a placement or a licence at the end. And I'd stop adding loan until I know what is real, because debt on a degree that doesn't pay is the worst thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum the truth, that I'm scared and I don't know. She'd say I should keep studying and she'd work more shifts, and that would make me feel worse. I wouldn't want her carrying me.

say: I'd say **two years** is reckless, and nobody has voted for it or prepared for it.
I'd demand an **emergency plan** for people's income first.
think: I'd have a **debt** and a degree for jobs that software does, and no family to catch me.
I'd feel I picked the **wrong thing** at the wrong time.
do: Ask the course office about **pausing** so I don't borrow more.
Look for any course with a **placement** or licence at the end.
feel: **Frightened**, and cheated after working hard for my grades.
S2.quote: I'd feel cheated, because I did everything right and worked hard for the grades.
fieldNote: First scenario where he **loses a plan**, not only worries about money.
Does not want his mother carrying him, which limits his support options.
Thinks in group and public solutions more than personal tactics.

steps.text: Ask the course office about pausing to stop more loan
Switch to a course with a placement and a licence
Go to every students' union meeting
Apply to the hardship fund for rent help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to organise, which I like. I'd say we need a campaign now, not after the layoffs. Unions in the care and public sectors would be where the jobs hold up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better than two, but not by much, because my degree ends in 2029 and AGI arrives in 2031. That's two years of trying to get hired into a market that's collapsing. I'd feel I'm just ahead of the wave and about to be hit by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree but change the direction. I'd choose modules on public policy and labour, and take a placement with a union or the council. I'd also finally learn how the tools work, because I can't argue against what I can't use. I'd keep one weekend shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit less panicky, more grim. Having a few years makes me feel I can do something, but I also know I'm not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you a graduation date inside the window. What changes compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be fighting to survive. With five, I can build a plan, and sit next to people who can help. It changes me from scared to determined, but still worried about the graduation year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the jobs just weren't there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that push it and the politicians who let them. I'd blame the ones who make the money, not the tools. And I'd blame the universities too if they keep taking fees for degrees they know are shrinking.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough to organise**, so we need a campaign now.
I'd say care and public-sector **unions** are where jobs will hold up.
think: My degree ends in **2029**, so I'd graduate into a market that is collapsing.
I can't argue against tools I **can't use**, so I should learn them.
do: Choose **public policy** and labour modules, and take a union placement.
Learn how the **AI tools** work, starting with one a week.
Keep one **weekend shift** and drop the other.
feel: Less panicky but **grim**, and more determined, because five years feels like something to use.
S3.quote: I'd blame the ones who make the money, not the tools. And I'd blame the universities too if they keep taking fees for degrees they know are shrinking.
fieldNote: The longer window moves him from **fear to organising**.
He accepts he must try the tools, which is a real shift for him.
Strong blame on firms and universities, none on the technology itself.

steps.text: Choose public policy and labour modules next year
Try one AI tool a week and note what it gets wrong
Take a placement with a union or the council
Keep the Saturday shift and drop Sunday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means we can actually vote on it. I'd say we should use the time for rules, public ownership of the big systems and a decent income floor. It would be a waste to spend it just sighing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels almost fine. I'd be about twenty-eight, with a career started and time to adapt. My worry is that people like me will be told to adapt alone, while the owners sit on the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, then probably do a master's in public policy while I still can. I'd get a job in the public sector or a union, and I'd learn the tools properly over time. I'd also help Mika choose subjects, because she has more time than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. There's enough time that I can believe in the plan. But I'd still be annoyed that ordinary people are expected to sort it out themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still do the same degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, but I'd add more practical skills early. Economics and politics help you understand what's happening. I'd just not count on a desk job at the end of it, and I'd have a second route ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for your mum and Mika?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That mum retires with her pension, Mika gets a fair start and none of us is begging. If the gains were shared, I'd be happy for the machines to do the boring parts. It's the sharing I don't trust.

say: I'd say **ten years** should go on rules, shared ownership and an **income floor**.
Spending the time sighing would be a waste.
think: Ten years feels nearly **fine**: I'd be twenty-eight with a career started.
My fear is people like me being told to **adapt alone** while owners keep the gains.
do: Finish the degree, then do a **master's** in public policy.
Aim for a **public sector** or union job.
Learn the **AI tools** properly over time and help my sister Mika choose subjects.
feel: **Calmer** than in the others, though annoyed that ordinary people must sort it out themselves.
S4.quote: I'd be happy for the machines to do the boring parts. It's the sharing I don't trust.
fieldNote: Time lets him **fear to planning**, with politics at the centre.
His distrust is about distribution, not about technology.
Thinks of his sister's future, which gives him a reason to stay calm.

steps.text: Apply for a master's in public policy after graduating
Volunteer for a policy campaign on income support
Learn one AI tool a term for coursework
Help Mika pick school subjects with lasting value

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one that worries me most is the two-year one. There'd be no time to plan, my debt would be sitting there, and my family has no cushion. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, a union that speaks for us and universities being honest about which jobs are real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that nobody asks first-year students like me what we think. We're told to be grateful for a place, and then the ground moves. I'd like someone to count us in.

headlineQuote: Nobody in my family has been to university, so I feel I have to make it count.
portrait: Jamal is an **18-year-old** politics and economics student on a scholarship, living at home and working weekends in a supermarket.
He never uses **AI tools**, distrusts firms, and turns first to unions and public support.
He is **anxious** about debt and entry jobs in most scenarios, and alarmed when AGI is only two years away.
With ten years to prepare he becomes calmer and plans a **master's** and a public sector career.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most: no time to plan, debt already owed, no family cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **income** while people retrain, a union voice and honest advice from universities.
